claim: Three synthetic single domain antibody libraries (concave, loop, and convex) were designed based on thermostabilized nanobody frameworks, each harboring a diversity of 9 × 10^12.
source: Three synthetic libraries exhibiting highly variable randomized surfaces (concave, loop and convex) each harboring a diversity of 9 × 1012 were designed based on thermostabilized nanobody frameworks.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the figure caption and supported by experimental data showing library construction and diversity measurements described in the methods section.

claim: The concave library is based on a GFP-binder nanobody (PDB: 3K1K) with a short CDR3 of six amino acids that binds via a concave surface.
source: The first template nanobody is a GFP-binder with a short CDR3 (six amino acids (aa) according to [Sircar et al., 2011]) that binds via a concave surface (PDB: 3K1K) (Kirchhofer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published structural data.

claim: The loop library is based on a β2-adrenergic receptor binder with a medium length CDR3 of 12 amino acids that inserts as an extended loop into a receptor cavity (PDB: 3P0G).
source: The second template is a β2-adrenergic receptor binder that inserts a medium length CDR3 (12 aa) as an extended loop into a receptor cavity (PDB: 3P0G) (Rasmussen et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published structural data.

claim: The convex library is based on a lysozyme binder with a long CDR3 of 16 amino acids that binds via a convex surface (PDB: 1ZVH).
source: The third template is a lysozyme binder displaying a long CDR3 (16 aa), which is tethered via an extended hydrophobic core, and binds via a convex surface (PDB: 1ZVH) (De Genst et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published structural data.

claim: The concave and loop libraries share the same framework because their template nanobodies 3K1K and 3P0G share high sequence identities.
source: Apart from the CDR regions, 3K1K and 3P0G share high sequence identities and therefore the concave and the loop library share the same framework (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The convex library has a different scaffold than the concave and loop libraries because 1ZVH contains an extended hydrophobic core.
source: In contrast, 1ZVH contains an extended hydrophobic core and the convex library was therefore built on a different scaffold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The concave framework sybody has a melting temperature of 74°C, representing a stability increase of 35°C compared to its natural precursor 3K1K.
source: They exhibited high melting temperatures of 74, 75 and 95°C for the concave, loop and convex scaffold, respectively, which corresponds to a stability increase of 21 to 35°C compared to their natural precursors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermofluor experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The loop framework sybody has a melting temperature of 75°C.
source: They exhibited high melting temperatures of 74, 75 and 95°C for the concave, loop and convex scaffold, respectively, which corresponds to a stability increase of 21 to 35°C compared to their natural precursors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermofluor experimental data.

claim: The convex framework sybody has a melting temperature of 95°C.
source: They exhibited high melting temperatures of 74, 75 and 95°C for the concave, loop and convex scaffold, respectively, which corresponds to a stability increase of 21 to 35°C compared to their natural precursors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermofluor experimental data.

claim: Three trinucleotide mixes were used for randomization at different positions: in loops, at transitions from loops to β-sheets, and in the middle of β-sheets.
source: Three trinucleotide mixes were used for randomized residues placed (i) in loops, (ii) at the transitions from loops to β-sheets and (iii) in the middle of β-sheets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by amino acid composition data in the referenced figure.

claim: Cysteines and prolines were excluded from all three trinucleotide randomization mixes.
source: Cysteines and prolines were generally excluded in any of the three mixes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the library design strategy.

claim: The theoretical diversity of the concave library is 8.3 × 10^17.
source: The theoretical diversity of the libraries amounts to 8.3 × 1017, 4.3 × 1019, and 2.8 × 1022 for the concave, loop and convex library, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and calculated based on the number of randomized positions.

claim: The theoretical diversity of the loop library is 4.3 × 10^19.
source: The theoretical diversity of the libraries amounts to 8.3 × 1017, 4.3 × 1019, and 2.8 × 1022 for the concave, loop and convex library, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and calculated based on the number of randomized positions.

claim: The theoretical diversity of the convex library is 2.8 × 10^22.
source: The theoretical diversity of the libraries amounts to 8.3 × 1017, 4.3 × 1019, and 2.8 × 1022 for the concave, loop and convex library, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and calculated based on the number of randomized positions.

claim: An experimental library diversity of 9 × 10^12 was determined for each of the three sybody libraries.
source: We determined an experimental library diversity of 9 × 1012 for each of the three libraries.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents measured experimental data.

claim: The PUREfrexSS kit contains oxidized glutathione (GSSG) and the disulfide bond isomerase DsbC, making it suited to support folding of disulfide-containing proteins.
source: The kit is devoid of reducing agents and contains oxidized glutathione (GSSG) and the disulfide bond isomerase DsbC and is thus suited to support the folding of disulfide-containing proteins such as nanobodies and sybodies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the properties of the commercial kit.

claim: More than 70% of input mRNA was translated in the ribosome display system using PUREfrexSS kit.
source: The analysis revealed that more than 70% of the input mRNA was translated.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Western blotting quantification data.

claim: Ribosome display of the 3K1K nanobody against GFP showed 84.6 ± 3.5% recovery of input mRNA.
source: For 3K1K panned against GFP, mRNA recovery was 84.6 ± 3.5%, while mRNA retrieved from 3K1K panning against MBP was not detectable.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Background binding of the non-randomized convex sybody to GFP and MBP was minimal with recovery fractions below 0.001%.
source: Background binding of the non-randomized convex sybody towards GFP and MBP was minimal (recovery fractions below 0.001%).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR data.

claim: Sybody selections against MBP using three rounds of ribosome display resulted in about 20%, 50%, and 30% ELISA-positive hits for the concave, loop, and convex libraries, respectively.
source: ELISA analysis of the selections of the concave, loop and convex library revealed about 20, 50 and 30% of all wells as strong and specific hits against MBP.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by ELISA data.

claim: Crystal structures of three convex MBP binders (Sb_MBP#1–3) in complex with MBP were solved at resolutions ranging from 1.4 to 1.9 Å.
source: Crystal structures of three convex MBP binders (Sb_MBP#1–3) in complex with MBP were solved at resolutions ranging from 1.4 to 1.9 Å (Figure 2, Table 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by crystallographic data in the referenced table.

claim: The structure of Sb_MBP#1 has an RMSD of 1.02 Å when compared to its natural precursor 1ZVH.
source: The structures of the crystallized sybodies were highly similar to their natural precursor (e.g. RMSD of 1.02 Å comparing Sb_MBP#1 and 1ZVH), thereby validating our library design, which kept selected residues of the CDRs constant to assure folding of an extended hydrophobic core (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: Sb_MBP#1–3 have binding affinities ranging from 24 to 500 nM as determined by surface plasmon resonance.
source: Sb_MBP#1–3 have binding affinities ranging from 24 to 500 nM as determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR measurements.

claim: Sb_MBP#1–3 bind into the cleft between the two lobes of MBP and trap the target in its ligand-free conformation.
source: They bind into the cleft between the two lobes of MBP and thereby trap the target in its ligand-free conformation (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (Spurlino et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by crystal structure data and citation to literature.

claim: A Schild plot analysis revealed 58-fold decreased sybody binding affinity at saturating maltose concentration.
source: A Schild plot analysis revealed 58-fold decreased sybody binding affinity at saturating maltose concentration and an affinity of 1.0 µM of MBP for maltose (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which is in close agreement with the literature (Telmer and Shilton, 2003).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR competition data and citation to literature.

claim: The affinity of MBP for maltose was determined as 1.0 µM.
source: A Schild plot analysis revealed 58-fold decreased sybody binding affinity at saturating maltose concentration and an affinity of 1.0 µM of MBP for maltose (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which is in close agreement with the literature (Telmer and Shilton, 2003).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR competition data and citation to literature.

claim: Three consecutive rounds of ribosome display were insufficient to obtain sybodies against the ABC transporter TM287/288.
source: Three consecutive rounds of ribosome display (analogous to the successful selections against MBP) were insufficient to obtain sybodies against membrane proteins, as we demonstrated at the example of the ABC transporter TM287/288 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data showing failed selection attempts.

claim: The sybody selection cascade combines one round of ribosome display followed by two rounds of phage display.
source: In its final form, the sybody platform is built as a selection cascade, starting with one round of ribosome display, followed by two rounds of phage display (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in the referenced figure.

claim: Immobilization surface chemistries are changed in every selection round of the sybody selection cascade.
source: Furthermore, immobilization surface chemistries are changed in every selection round.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the selection protocol.

claim: TM287/288 almost exclusively adopts an inward-facing state in the absence of ATP.
source: In the absence of ATP, the bacterial ABC transporter TM287/288 almost exclusively adopts an inward-facing (IF) state, and two crystal structures were solved in this conformation (Hohl et al., 2012; Hohl et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published crystal structures.

claim: The transition of TM287/288 to the outward-facing state requires ATP binding.
source: The transition to the OF state requires ATP binding (Figure 3A) (Timachi et al., 2017), but ATP hydrolysis constantly reverts the transporter back to its IF state.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published work.

claim: The E517A mutation in TM287/288 blocks ATP hydrolysis without impairing ATP binding.
source: In order to populate the OF state, a glutamate to alanine substitution (E517A) in the ATP-binding cassette was introduced, which blocks ATP hydrolysis without impairing ATP binding (Timachi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published work.

claim: Sybody selections against TM287/288(E517A) in the presence of ATP showed enrichment of 170, 220, and 25 fold for the concave, loop, and convex libraries, respectively, after the second round of phage display.
source: Using qPCR and AcrB as background control (Seeger et al., 2013), we observed strong sybody enrichment of 170, 220 and 25 fold for the concave, loop and convex library, respectively, after the second round of phage display.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR data.

claim: 60% of clones analyzed by ELISA from TM287/288 selections were ELISA positive.
source: For each library, 190 clones were analyzed for binding against TM287/288(E517A) in the presence of ATP by ELISA, of which 60% were ELISA positive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by ELISA data.

claim: Of 48 sequenced ELISA hits from TM287/288 selections, 40 were unique.
source: Of 48 sequenced ELISA hits, 40 were unique, indicating high diversity after binder selection (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequencing data.

claim: 37 of 40 unique sybodies against TM287/288 could be purified at sufficient yields and quality for further analyses.
source: The unique sybodies were named Sb_TM#1–40, and 37 thereof could be purified at sufficient yields and quality for further analyses.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the purification results.

claim: 11 sybodies against TM287/288 were specific for the outward-facing state as defined by an affinity increase of at least ten-fold upon addition of ATP.
source: SPR data of 31 binders could be quantified and revealed 11 sybodies specific for OF TM287/288(E517A) as defined by an affinity increase of at least ten-fold upon addition of ATP (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Sb_TM#26 exhibited exclusive binding to TM287/288 only in the presence of ATP.
source: Sb_TM#26 exhibited a particularly strong state-specificity as binding was exclusively detected in the presence of ATP.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR data.

claim: Sb_TM#26 inhibits ATP hydrolysis of TM287/288 with an IC50 of 62 nM.
source: Therefore, this binder was analyzed for its capacity to inhibit ATP hydrolysis of TM287/288, revealing an IC50 of ATP hydrolysis of 62 nM (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by ATPase activity assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Multiple attempts to raise mouse antibodies or nanobodies against ENT1 and GlyT1 by immunizations failed.
source: Multiple attempts to raise mouse antibodies or nanobodies against these targets by immunizations failed in our hands, presumably due to low thermal target stability and the limited number of accessible epitopes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing unsuccessful immunization attempts.

claim: Sybody selections against ENT1 were performed at 4°C in the presence of the inhibitor NBTI.
source: In order to obtain conformation-specific binders against ENT1 and GlyT1, we performed selections at 4°C in the presence of the inhibitors S-(4-Nitrobenzyl)−6-thioinosine (NBTI) and a Bitopertin-like molecule named Cmpd1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the selection conditions.

claim: Sybody selections against GlyT1 were performed at 4°C in the presence of the inhibitor Cmpd1.
source: In order to obtain conformation-specific binders against ENT1 and GlyT1, we performed selections at 4°C in the presence of the inhibitors S-(4-Nitrobenzyl)−6-thioinosine (NBTI) and a Bitopertin-like molecule named Cmpd1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the selection conditions.

claim: For ENT1, the concave but not the convex and loop library was enriched 4-fold over background after binder selection.
source: For ENT1, the concave but not the convex and loop library was enriched 4-fold over background after binder selection.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by enrichment data.

claim: One concave sybody called Sb_ENT1#1 was identified against ENT1 with an affinity of 40 nM.
source: One concave sybody called Sb_ENT1#1 was identified by ELISA and purified as monodisperse protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). SPR measurements revealed an affinity of 40 nM (Figure 5B, Table 5).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR data shown in the referenced figure and table.

claim: Sb_ENT1#1 binding led to an increase in ENT1 melting temperature by 6.1°C as measured by thermal shift scintillation proximity assay.
source: Sb_ENT1#1 binding led to a sharper transition trajectory and an increase in melting temperature by 6.1°C (Figure 5C), indicating that sybody binding increases the population of the inhibited conformation of ENT1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPA-TS data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The absolute binding signal for NBTI to ENT1 was increased by more than seven-fold in the presence of Sb_ENT1#1 at temperatures well below Tm.
source: Supporting this notion, the absolute binding signal for NBTI was increased by more than seven-fold in the presence of Sb_ENT1#1 at temperatures well below Tm (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPA data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Seven sybodies from the concave (Sb_GlyT1#1–4) and loop (Sb_GlyT1#5–7) libraries were identified against GlyT1.
source: For GlyT1, seven sybodies from the concave (Sb_GlyT1#1–4) and loop (Sb_GlyT1#5–7) library were identified by ELISA and complex formation was confirmed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by ELISA and SEC data.

claim: GlyT1 sybodies have binding affinities ranging from 494 pM to 2.52 µM as determined by SPR.
source: Binding kinetics were determined by SPR revealing a wide range of affinities from 494 pM to 2.52 µM (Figure 6C and D, Table 5, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPR data shown in the referenced figures and table.

claim: Competition binding SPR analysis revealed that concave sybodies Sb_GlyT1#1–4 bind to a different epitope than loop sybodies Sb_GlyT1#5 and Sb_GlyT1#7.
source: Competition binding SPR analysis using GlyT1 pre-saturated with Sb_GlyT1#6 revealed binding of concave sybodies Sb_GlyT1#1–4 but not of loop sybodies Sb_GlyT1#5 and Sb_GlyT1#7 (Figure 6E), demonstrating that at least two non-overlapping epitopes on GlyT1 are recognized.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by competition SPR data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Sb_GlyT1#6 and Sb_GlyT1#7 stabilized GlyT1 by 8.8 and 10°C, respectively, as measured by SPA-TS.
source: Of the seven sybodies, Sb_GlyT1#1–5 increased the Tm by 0.9–2.6°C, whereas Sb_GlyT1#6 and Sb_GlyT1#7 stabilized the transporter by 8.8 and 10°C, respectively (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPA-TS data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: All GlyT1 sybodies stabilize the inhibited conformation of GlyT1 as evidenced by increased absolute SPA binding signals.
source: Absolute SPA binding signals obtained at 19°C increased up to 1.8-fold (Sb_GlyT1#7), suggesting that all sybodies stabilize the inhibited conformation of GlyT1 (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPA data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The sybody platform does not require access to animal facilities and builds exclusively on commercially available reagents.
source: The platform does not require access to animal facilities and builds exclusively on commercially available reagents, thus enabling every lab to rapidly generate binders against challenging membrane proteins.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the description of methods using commercial reagents.

claim: Sybodies can be generated within three weeks from selection to preparative production.
source: Our approach permits the selection and preparative production of sybodies within three weeks and requires only standard laboratory materials.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the timeline of the platform.

claim: The sybody platform allows for full control over the binder selection process including selection in the presence of ligands.
source: Pure in vitro binder selection methods in theory can overcome these drawbacks of immunization, because they allow for the full control over the binder selection process.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by examples of selections performed in the presence of specific ligands.

claim: Ribosome display allows displaying 10^12 different library members with minor experimental effort.
source: In contrast to the widely used phage and yeast display systems, which have maximal library sizes of 109–1010 members, ribosome display offers the advantage of displaying 1012 different library members with minor experimental effort.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text comparing different display technologies.

claim: Phage and yeast display libraries are typically limited to 10^8–10^10 library members.
source: In contrast to the widely used phage and yeast display systems, which have maximal library sizes of 109–1010 members, ribosome display offers the advantage of displaying 1012 different library members with minor experimental effort.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text comparing different display technologies.

claim: The initial ribosome display round generates a sybody pool with a maximal diversity of 5 × 10^6.
source: By systematically monitoring output cDNA amounts using qPCR, we learned that the initial ribosome display round generates a sybody pool with a maximal diversity of 5 × 106, from which a focused phage display library can be constructed with moderate effort in analogy to nanobody cloning from B-cells of immunized camelids (Pardon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR monitoring data.

claim: The sybody vectors were made available through Addgene.
source: In order to facilitate the spread and further development of the technology, the libraries will be made fully available to academic labs and the phage display and sybody expression vectors were made available through Addgene.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Addgene IDs provided in the tables.

claim: Natural nanobodies from camelids with CDR3 loops ≥16 amino acids always feature an extended hydrophobic core to tether CDR3.
source: Importantly, natural nanobodies from camelids with CDR3 loops ≥ 16 aa always feature an extended hydrophobic core to tether CDR3 (Sircar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published structural analysis.

claim: Many natural nanobodies with long CDR3 loops contain a second disulfide bond to restrict the flexibility of the long CDR3 loops.
source: In addition, many of them contain a second disulfide bond to restrict the flexibility of the long CDR3 loops (Sircar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published structural analysis.

claim: The convex sybody library is currently the only synthetic nanobody library with a long CDR3 that mimics loop tethering as found in camelid nanobodies.
source: Hence, our convex sybody library is currently the only synthetic nanobody library with a long CDR3 that mimics loop tethering as found in camelid nanobodies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparison with other published synthetic nanobody libraries.

claim: The structures of convex sybody/MBP complexes revealed binding via the designed convex surfaces into a cleft of the target protein.
source: In contrast, the structures of our convex sybody/MBP complexes revealed binding via the designed convex surfaces into a cleft of the target protein, thus confirming the anticipated binding mode.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by crystal structure data.

claim: Decreased surface hydrophobicity was previously demonstrated in a DARPin library to be of paramount importance to counteract the enrichment of sticky binders when selecting against membrane proteins.
source: Decreased surface hydrophobicity was previously demonstrated in a DARPin library to be of paramount importance to counteract the enrichment of sticky binders when selecting against membrane proteins (Seeger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to published work.

claim: The sybody-MBP structures have been deposited at the Protein Data Bank under the accession codes 5M13, 5M14 and 5M15.
source: The sybody-MBP structures have been deposited at the Protein Data Bank under the accession codes 5M13, 5M14 and 5M15.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the data availability section.

claim: Immunizations are limited to comparatively stable proteins because delicate targets readily unfold upon injection due to applied adjuvants and the camelid's high body temperature.
source: First, the target space is limited to comparatively stable proteins, because delicate targets (e.g. many human membrane transporters) readily unfold upon injection due to the applied adjuvants and the camelid's high body temperature.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of immunization approaches.

claim: It is very difficult to favor target conformations with non-covalent ligands during immunization because they dissociate from the protein shortly after injection unless their affinities are extremely high.
source: Second, it is very difficult to favor target conformations with non-covalent ligands because they dissociate from the protein shortly after injection, unless their affinities are extremely high, as was the case for the β2 adrenergic receptor agonist BI-167107 having a dissociation constant of as low as 84 pM (Rasmussen et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to a specific example.

claim: Immunizations require access to animal facilities, which makes it difficult and expensive for many researchers to implement binder generation on a routine basis.
source: Third, immunizations require access to animal facilities, which makes it difficult and expensive for many researchers to implement binder generation on a routine basis in their own lab.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of immunization approaches.

claim: There are only a few published examples from specialized labs reporting on successful in vitro selections against integral membrane proteins.
source: However, in praxis there are only a few published examples from specialized labs reporting on successful in vitro selections against integral membrane proteins (Dominik et al., 2016; Kodan et al., 2014; Seeger et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2014; Uysal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published examples.

claim: Many prominent examples of membrane protein binders resulted from immunizations rather than in vitro selections.
source: This stands in contrast to many prominent examples of membrane protein binders that resulted from immunizations (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012; Liang et al., 2017; Rasmussen et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published examples.

claim: Small library sizes of 10^9–10^10 for phage or yeast display can result in weak binding affinities.
source: Potential limitations of synthetic binders are (i) small library sizes (namely 109–1010 for phage or yeast display), which can result in weak binding affinities
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of in vitro selection methods.

claim: Sub-optimal framework design can give rise to aggregated or poorly expressing library members.
source: (ii) sub-optimal framework design, which can give rise to aggregated or poorly expressing library members
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of synthetic binder libraries.

claim: Selection bias as a consequence of binder display and target immobilization can lead to poorly enriched binder pools.
source: (iii) selection bias as a consequence of binder display and target immobilization, which can lead to poorly enriched binder pools (Bradbury et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Extensive binder screening and purification efforts are often required after in vitro selection to identify suitable binders.
source: Consequently, extensive binder screening and purification efforts are often required after selection to identify suitable binders, as was for example the case for DARPin selections against the ABC transporters MsbA and LmrCD carried out in our lab (Mittal et al., 2012; Seeger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published examples.

claim: Conformation-specific binders raised against membrane proteins have the ability to manipulate cells directly at the cell surface.
source: Conformation-specific binders raised against membrane proteins have the ability to manipulate cells directly at the cell surface and are exquisite tools for basic science and drug discovery (Ahuja et al., 2015; Blanpain et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Binder selection against membrane proteins is very challenging because membrane proteins tend to be flexible, exhibit only small hydrophilic surfaces, require detergents or lipids to remain folded and are typically obtained only in small amounts.
source: However, binder selection against this difficult class of target proteins is very challenging (Dominik et al., 2016; Doshi et al., 2014; Pardon et al., 2014), because membrane proteins tend to be flexible, exhibit only small hydrophilic surfaces, require detergents or lipids to remain folded and are typically obtained only in small amounts.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The success of nanobodies is rooted in the simplicity and robustness of the VHH scaffold and in its characteristic variability at CDR3.
source: The success of nanobodies is rooted in the simplicity and robustness of the VHH scaffold and in its characteristic variability at the complementarity determining region 3 (CDR3), which is frequently found to penetrate deeply into cavities of membrane protein targets (Kruse et al., 2013; Rasmussen et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to structural examples.

claim: CDR3 loops of variable length and orientation create diverse binder shapes, thus permitting an optimal surface-complementarity to antigens.
source: CDR3 loops of variable length and orientation create diverse binder shapes, thus permitting an optimal surface-complementarity to antigens.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the structural basis for nanobody binding diversity.

claim: There are only a small number of approved drugs or drugs in development which therapeutically target human SLC transporters.
source: There are only a small number of approved drugs or drugs in development, which therapeutically target human SLC transporters, indicating untapped potential (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Human SLC transporters are notoriously difficult to work with in early drug discovery stages due to their intricate architecture and low thermal stability.
source: A main reason behind these shortcomings is the intricate architecture and low thermal stability that makes human SLC transporters notoriously difficult to work with in early drug discovery stages (César-Razquin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: ENT1 is involved in ischemia and acts as a biomarker in pancreatic cancer.
source: Here we focus on two transporters with a high need for conformation-specific binders for the screening of small molecule therapeutics, namely the equilibrative nucleoside transporter 1 (ENT1, SLC29A1) that is involved in ischemia and acts as a biomarker in pancreatic cancer (Yang and Leung, 2015)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: GlyT1 plays an important role in diseases of the central and peripheral nervous system.
source: as well as on the glycine transporter 1 (GlyT1, SLC6A9) that plays an important role in diseases of the central and peripheral nervous system (Harvey and Yee, 2013)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: The identified sybodies against ENT1 and GlyT1 trap inhibited conformations and thereby enhance ligand binding.
source: The identified binders trap inhibited conformations of ENT1 and GlyT1 and thereby enhance ligand binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by SPA-TS data showing increased ligand binding.

claim: The sybodies against ENT1 and GlyT1 increase assay sensitivity for inhibitor screening and can serve as crystallization chaperones for structure-based drug design.
source: Hence, these binders increase assay sensitivity for inhibitor screening and can serve as crystallization chaperones for structure-based drug design.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents an inference from the demonstrated stabilization and enhanced ligand binding properties.

claim: Binder generation against challenging membrane proteins benefits from radical changes in display format and target immobilization between each selection round to overcome selection biases.
source: We further realized that binder generation against challenging membrane proteins benefits from radical changes in display format and target immobilization between each selection round to overcome otherwise inevitable biases.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data comparing different selection protocols.

claim: Libraries based on synthetic scaffolds often exhibit a single shape and are randomized at only one region of their surface.
source: Libraries based on synthetic scaffolds often exhibit a single shape and are randomized at only one region of their surface.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing limitations of existing synthetic binder libraries.

claim: Suboptimal shape-complementarity between the randomized binder surface and the few accessible epitopes on membrane proteins is a key limiting factor that can impede successful selections.
source: Since a large fraction of the membrane protein surface is buried beneath lipids or detergent micelles, suboptimal shape-complementarity between its few accessible epitopes and the randomized binder surface is a key limiting factor that can impede successful selections.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing challenges in membrane protein binder selection.

claim: Three synthetic single domain antibody libraries of different shapes were engineered to create a large paratope space, which is a key feature to target membrane proteins with a limited number of suitable epitopes.
source: To overcome this barrier, we engineered three synthetic single domain antibody libraries of different shapes, a strategy that had been applied previously to monobodies and DARPins (Koide et al., 2012; Schilling et al., 2014). Thereby, we created a large paratope space, which is a key feature of the sybody platform to target membrane proteins with a limited number of suitable epitopes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to similar strategies used for other scaffolds.

claim: Each nanobody contains a dedicated set of aromatic or aliphatic CDR residues which point towards its hydrophobic core and thereby contribute to scaffold stability.
source: A thorough investigation of published nanobody structures revealed that each nanobody contains a dedicated set of aromatic or aliphatic CDR residues, which point towards its hydrophobic core and thereby contribute to scaffold stability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents an inference from structural analysis.

claim: Scaffolding CDR residues are harmonized among CDRs of the same nanobody but vary among different camelid nanobodies.
source: Importantly, scaffolding CDR residues are harmonized among CDRs of the same nanobody (see for example 1ZVH and convex library), but vary among different camelid nanobodies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural analysis.

claim: CDRs of nanobodies cannot be exchanged without the risk of destabilizing the scaffold.
source: Consequently, CDRs of nanobodies cannot be exchanged without the risk of destabilizing the scaffold.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents an inference from the observation about scaffolding residues.

claim: The three sybody scaffolds were engineered based on individual nanobody structures to achieve high thermal stability.
source: We took this into account by engineering the three sybody scaffolds based on individual nanobody structures. Thereby, we achieved high thermal stability of the sybodies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermofluor data showing high melting temperatures.

claim: Structure-based scaffold designs had been successfully applied in the past to construct Fab, monobody, and anticalin libraries.
source: Structure-based scaffold designs had been successfully applied in the past to construct Fab libraries based on the highly stable humanized Fab-4D5 fragment (Fellouse et al., 2004), monobody libraries on the tenth FN3 unit of human fibronectin (Koide et al., 1998) and anticalin libraries based on the human lipocalin protein Lcn2 (Schönfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published examples.

claim: Large binder diversities are critical for in vitro selections to compensate for affinity maturation taking place in animals as a result of somatic hypermutation.
source: Besides the favorable biophysical library properties, large binder diversities are critical for in vitro selections, in order to compensate for affinity maturation taking place in animals as a result of somatic hypermutation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established knowledge about antibody maturation.
